title: The Calendar of Offerings: Daily, Weekly, Monthly
summary: God gives Moses a schedule of public offerings for Israel's worship in the land. Every day a lamb is offered in the morning and at twilight; every Sabbath two more lambs are added; at every new moon larger offerings are made. The chapter then sets out the offerings for Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and for the day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks.
story: With a new generation counted (chapter 26) and a new leader named (chapter 27), Numbers turns to the rhythm of life Israel must keep once it settles in the land. Chapters 28 and 29 belong together as one calendar, moving from the daily offering outward to the great festivals of the year. Many of these feasts were already commanded in Exodus 23 and Leviticus 23, but those passages focused on the people's rest and celebration. Here the focus is the public offerings the priests must present on behalf of the whole nation. Placed at this point in the book, the calendar is an act of hope: God speaks of Sabbaths, new moons, and harvests in a land Israel does not yet hold, as though settlement were already certain.
historical:
The chapter assumes the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary built at Sinai, and a functioning priesthood under Eleazar. Verse 6 notes that the daily burnt offering was “established at Mount Sinai”, referring back to Exodus 29:38-42. The same regular offering continued later in Solomon's temple and in the second temple after the exile. Its interruption was a sign of catastrophe: the book of Daniel describes a hostile king who would take away the regular burnt offering (Daniel 8:11), which Jewish readers connected with Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple in 167 BC. After the Romans destroyed the temple in AD 70, the offerings ceased, and Jewish worship reorganized around prayer, with the daily services understood as corresponding to the times of the daily offerings.

Israel's months were lunar, beginning with the new moon. The first month (later called Nisan, falling in March or April) was the month of Passover, and the Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later at the end of the grain harvest, in late spring.
cultural:
An ancient reader would have taken for granted that a god's temple required regular provision. Across the ancient Near East, temples offered daily meals to the gods' images, and texts from Mesopotamia and Egypt describe elaborate menus served to deities morning and evening. Israel's system shares some of this vocabulary: the offerings are called “the food for My offerings by fire.” But there is no image in Israel's sanctuary to be fed, and elsewhere the psalmist has God say that he does not need his people's bulls or goats (Psalm 50:9-13). The language of food and pleasing aroma expresses fellowship and acceptance, not divine hunger.

The components of each offering are carefully proportioned. Each animal comes with a grain offering of fine flour mixed with olive oil and a drink offering of wine, and the amounts scale with the size of the animal: more for a bull, less for a ram, least for a lamb. An ephah was a dry measure (roughly a bushel or somewhat less; estimates vary) and a hin a liquid measure of a few liters. Bread, oil, and wine were the staples of the land's agriculture, so the offerings brought the produce of Israel's fields to God along with its animals.
literary: The chapter is a liturgical calendar written as divine instruction, and its style is deliberately repetitive. The same phrases return again and again: “a pleasing aroma”, “an offering made by fire”, “unblemished”, and “in addition to the regular burnt offering.” That last phrase is the structural key. Every special offering is added on top of the daily one, so that the calendar builds in layers: day, Sabbath, month, and then the yearly feasts. The order is from the most frequent to the least, and from the ordinary to the festival, and chapter 29 continues the same pattern into the seventh month. Reading it aloud, one hears how worship was meant to fill Israel's time, with nothing left outside the sound of it.

outline.t: Present the offerings at their appointed times
The daily offering, morning and evening
The offering at each new moon
Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
The day of firstfruits at the Feast of Weeks

doctrines.note: Every animal must be unblemished, and every offering is presented at its appointed time. God's holiness shapes not only special occasions but the ordinary rhythm of every day.

Alongside the burnt offerings of devotion, the new moon and each festival include a male goat as a sin offering “to make atonement for you.” Even Israel's joyful feasts assume that a sinful people needs its sin dealt with before it can draw near.

The daily morning and evening offering gave Israel a fixed rhythm of worship. Later generations patterned their times of prayer on it, and Psalm 141:2 asks that the psalmist's prayer be counted as incense and his lifted hands as the evening sacrifice.

words.note: Tamid, continually or regular. Used here as a noun for the regular burnt offering, the daily lamb offered morning and evening. The word stresses constancy: this offering never stops, and every other offering is added to it. In later Jewish tradition the daily offering was known simply as the Tamid.

Nichoach, soothing or pleasing, used in the phrase a pleasing aroma. The expression first appears after the flood, when God smells Noah's offering (Genesis 8:21). It describes an offering that God accepts with favor. Paul uses the same picture of Christ, who gave himself as a fragrant offering to God (Ephesians 5:2).

Olah, burnt offering, literally what goes up. The whole animal was burned on the altar, and nothing was kept by the priest or the worshiper. It expressed total devotion to God and was also understood to make atonement (Leviticus 1:4). It is the backbone of the calendar in this chapter.

christ: The New Testament reads the whole system of regular offerings as pointing forward to a single sacrifice that would end the need for repetition. Hebrews contrasts the priests who stand daily offering sacrifices with Christ: “Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11-12). The festivals in this chapter also mark the Gospel story. Jesus was crucified at Passover, and Paul calls him our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). The Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Weeks, called Pentecost in Greek, fifty days after Passover (Acts 2:1). Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20), drawing on the harvest offering named in verse 26. These links are ones the New Testament makes, reading the calendar in light of Christ.
questions: Israel's worship began with a daily offering, morning and evening, before any festival. What daily rhythms shape your life, and what would it mean for them to include God?
Every special offering was made in addition to the regular one, never in place of it. How might this pattern speak to the relationship between ordinary faithfulness and special occasions?
The calendar was given before Israel had any land to farm. What does it say about God's promises that he taught his people to plan their harvest festivals in advance?
